items.why: The sword command directly targets her followers, but the woman’s later execution makes the competitor somewhat plausible.
Ishbi-Benob threatens David, whereas Abishai rescues David by killing Ishbi-Benob.
The king requests prayer, but the man of God is the one who intercedes.
Elisha’s reply to the officer’s doubt is the warning that he will see the food but not eat it, not the earlier price prophecy.
Reporting to the palace is the new plan after their admission; hiding the goods was already completed.
The ordered battle accounts clearly place Sibbekai’s killing before Elhanan’s.
The stated reason is the Lord’s command, though this is explicit and the competitor merely misreads a concessive offer.
The passage distinguishes the three peoples God helped Uzziah fight from the Ammonites who paid tribute.
Jeroboam does not change his ways but does appoint priests again, creating a clear polarity distinction.
Azariah and the priests are the followers, and Uzziah is the person they follow into the temple.
Making Uzziah king is the purpose of taking him; Amaziah’s death is background circumstance, though take is slightly stiff wording.
The letter heading clearly distinguishes Claudius Lysias as sender from Felix as addressee.
Resolving the quoted pronouns shows that the speaking woman’s son was eaten first.
The prophet brings the body to his city before later placing it in his tomb.
Paul talks until daylight immediately before leaving; breaking bread occurs earlier.
The two centurions receive the command, while the soldiers and others form the detachment they must prepare.
Within the king’s account of the plan, the Arameans expect to enter the city after capturing those who emerge.
The contrastive clause sends the cavalry onward while the remaining soldiers return to the barracks.
Evil spirits are explicitly said to leave, but the items’ arrival is an unnatural and indirect description of the event.
The detailed duty assignments distinguish the two normally off-duty companies as those told to guard the temple for the king.
The governing pronoun refers to Uzziah, distinguishing his love of soil from the laborers’ work.
The final sentence directly attributes all four defeats to David and his men; Jonathan is named for only one.
The conspirators are waiting for the commander’s consent and intend to kill Paul before he reaches the Sanhedrin.
Paul’s impending departure is an explicit reason, while the lamps have no plausible causal role.
The quoted pronouns place the speaking woman’s child today and the other woman’s child tomorrow, though other woman is mildly perspective-dependent.
The imperative Seize him targets the man of God, not the king who issues it.
The messengers’ return and report immediately precede the people’s plundering of the camp.
The messenger’s master and the planned beheading identify the king, rather than the messenger, as the murderer Elisha means.
The passage explicitly grounds Uzziah’s eagerness in the Lord’s affliction, distinct from the priests hurrying him out.
The sequence clearly has Ben-Hadad mobilize his army before marching and laying siege.
Zechariah directly instructs Uzziah in reverence for God; Amaziah is only the father whose conduct Uzziah follows.
The practitioners burn the scrolls immediately after gathering them; valuation happens afterward.
The trampled person is the officer assigned to the gate, not the king who assigned him.
The warning is addressed to the man of God from Judah, despite being delivered through the old prophet.
The accusers are ordered to present their case; the Sanhedrin is only the earlier forum.
Jehoiada gives the weapons, while David is identified only as their former owner.
Hearing the noise causes Athaliah to go to the crowd; seeing the king occurs only after she arrives.
The passage explicitly links the city’s calm to Athaliah’s death, not merely to the people’s rejoicing.
The 2,600 family leaders command the army; Jeiel and Maaseiah are involved in mustering and administration.
The sons saddle the donkey, but the old prophet is the one who mounts it.
The answer news is an abstract placeholder that does not identify the reported content and offers little discrimination.
The pronouns them and they refer to the seven sons who are beaten and flee, not to the attacking man.
The Arameans imagine the hired Hittite and Egyptian kings as the attackers, while Israel’s king is the supposed hirer.
The continuing pronouns refer to the departing man of God, distinguishing him from the prophet who saddled the donkey.
The fulfilled warning applies to the doubting officer, who is trampled, rather than to the man of God who warned him.
Paul explicitly says that the young man has information for the commander.
Within the old prophet’s claimed message, him refers to the man of God who is to return and eat.
The final sequence places Jotham’s succession after Uzziah’s burial, whereas Isaiah’s record is mentioned earlier.
The prophecy makes the named son Josiah the agent who will sacrifice the priests; Jeroboam is merely present at the altar.
The Sanhedrin is to petition, but the commander is the person expected to bring Paul.
The old prophet predicts fulfillment of a message declared by the man of God, but the question’s he and gives the message are awkwardly ambiguous.
Joash is Ahaziah’s son and is explicitly hidden with his nurse; Ahaziah is already dead.
The men reject both staying and entering the city, then decide to surrender at the Aramean camp.
The first covenant includes the Lord, king, and people, clearly distinguished from the subsequent king-and-people covenant.
